Article Title: From uplifting heartbroken team to calling out Chess Olympiad hotel mess: Srinath is India's man to count on
Article Text:
Srinath Narayanan is India's man to count on

Srinath with Nihal Sarin

Srinath was there; he is here too

The captain on India's Olympiad prep

All eyes will be on Gukesh (FIDE Photo)

From rapid back to classical

NEW DELHI: It was the final round of the Global Chess League (GCL) round-robin last Saturday in Bengaluru, and American Gambits needed a big win, with an eight-point margin, to reach the final. Mumba Masters were the opponents. As the match wore on, the Gambits, playing with Black, went all out. Javokhir Sindarov, playing on the Icon board, won his game. On the next board, Indian grandmaster Nihal Sarin had an early advantage, which translated almost into a winning position. But then, calamity struck.The clock ran out. Sarin lost on time. His team lost with him.The next moment, Nihal was pressed against the side glass of the dugout, face to the panel, looking as though the gates might open and the tears might come at any second. Then he felt a palm settle lightly on his shoulder. It was none other than the Gambits' captain and coach, Srinath Narayanan."It was very painful," Srinath told TimesofIndia.com later during an exclusive interaction. "You usually need some time and space for the emotions to dial down. And I think that's pretty much the only thing that can heal things."There was no tactical debrief that night, no post-mortem of the time scramble.Srinath took the squad out for a team dinner instead. Later, back at the hotel, they pulled out board games, like Salem and Avalon, and played into the night."We tried to take our minds off these things," Srinath recalled with a smile. "And then at night, we played some fun games that helped us cope with it."The response the next day suggested it had worked. Facing the same Mumba Masters in the third-place match, the Gambits crushed them across both legs. Nihal won both his games. The Gambits took bronze."We are overall quite happy, because it would have been very depressing and disappointing if we had lost today," Srinath said, acknowledging his team's performance in GCL 2026. "But it also feels like a slight underachievement given the potential of the team.""We felt like we were definitely one of the contenders for winning the tournament. And we played that way for the most part. So we just lost out on those last two matches, where things got decided at the very end, in the last few seconds."This is a man who knows what winning a team event actually looks like and what it takes to do so. When India took gold in Budapest at the 2024 Olympiad, Srinath was there.He was there, too, on Tuesday, when the Indian contingent landed in Samarkand for the 46th Olympiad and found themselves stranded without accommodation. And he was the first to break the silence publicly."Having a terrible experience at the FIDE 2026 Olympiad," he wrote on X. "The team landed 5 hours ago at Samarkand airport. The team still haven't been allotted rooms, with absolutely no clarity on when it'll be allotted." As TimesofIndia.com reported later in the evening , the players were eventually given individual rooms. The coaching staff were put into shared rooms for the time being.When the suspense over India's board order finally lifted, the team going with a straight rating-wise arrangement, putting Praggnanandhaa (2761) on Board 1, Arjun Erigaisi (2759) on Board 2, Nihal (2718) on Board 3, D Gukesh (2703) on Board 4 and Vidit Gujrathi (2697) on Board 5, Srinath took to X again, this time with rather more mischief."Don't blame me for keeping the board order in suspense. I had it on chess-results right from September 1," he penned.Preparation for the Olympiad had already begun well before the GCL gig, in the form of a virtual camp with the full squad.When asked how it went, he replied, "It went really well. As a unit, we gelled really well. The players are all around similar ages. And we have Vidit, who is quite experienced but still not quite that old."One of the sources of encouragement for the 32-year-old Grandmaster was that three of his Olympiad squad, Nihal, Arjun and Vidit, had all been in Bengaluru, and all three finished with positive scores in the tournament."It's pretty encouraging that the three players who are here played quite well," Srinath told this website. "All of them with positive scores. I think that's also an encouraging sign for the team."In general, the fact that we can all be friends with each other, we can have a fun time even outside of the tournament, I think that's a really special thing about Olympiad."There is one obvious wrinkle in going straight from a rapid-format league into the sport's biggest classical team event. And Srinath doesn't dismiss it."It definitely can take a game or two to get back," he admitted. "But it won't take longer than that."In general, at the Olympiad, the first few rounds are not the most challenging rounds. So it gives us plenty of time to acclimatise."And the composition of his squad helps more."The younger you are, the easier it is to adapt," he said, a useful trait in a team where four of the five boards are occupied by players in their early twenties or younger.Srinath has spent this fortnight uplifting a devastated dressing room, calling out a governing body over a logistical mess, and cheekily reminding everyone on social media that he'd had India's board order published for weeks.In Samarkand, this is the man India counts on to do all of it again.
Article Summary: Srinath Narayanan is captain of India's chess team at the FIDE 2026 Olympiad in Samarkand. Gambits lost in the final of the Global Chess League (GCL) round- robin in Bengaluru. Srinath: "We felt like we were definitely one of the contenders for winning the tournament"

Article Title: Sanju Samson's blitz against Afghanistan keeps Vaibhav Sooryavanshi waiting - and the debate alive
Article Text:
Sanju Samson (PTI photo)

New Delhi:

Sanju Samson

Poll Vote & Share your view Who should be given more chances in the T20 format? Sanju Samson Vaibhav Sooryavanshi Abhishek Sharma 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Mohammad Nabi moved to his left, leaped ever so slightly at the long-off boundary rope, got his hands underneath the leather and held on. A few inches more and the ball would have possibly evaded him for a six. Instead, he gestured 'out' to the umpire and a probing Rashid Khan . The Afghanistan spinner checked if the foot was planted safely and comfortably inside the field of play. The moment he got the nod, the 27-year-old went on to celebrate his second wicket of the over. Sanju Samson walked back after scoring 57 runs from 22 balls, hitting seven fours and four sixes along the way.As far as rubber stamping their places go, this was Samson's attempt - with 52 of his 57 runs coming in boundaries. In a game of musical chairs that he's been involved in with Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, Samson has, arguably, had the raw end of the deal. And here he was, suggesting once again that he wasn't going away easily.On the back of a stellar T20 World Cup, playing a huge role in India winning the trophy, he was benched unceremoniously after a poor showing against Ireland. In came Sooryavanshi, who didn't hit the ground running on his inauguration to the international stage.Samson then returned for the last two T20I against England before missing the flight to Zimbabwe. There, Sooryavanshi who went hammer and tongs and emerged as the Player of the Match.Yet, as the T20I series against Afghanistan rolled around, Samson was picked to open the innings alongside Abhishek Sharma . He started the series with just 10 before producing the goods in the second contest.Azmatullah Omarzai and Mohammad Nabi bore the bulk of his prolific shot-making at the Arun Jaitley Stadium on Tuesday. The former conceded 23 from 10 balls while the latter went for 22 from seven deliveries. The aspect that stood out, and stands out in most Samson knocks, is the ease with which he clear the in-field.An overpitched start to the fifth over by Omarzai was sent over the mid-on fielder. Next ball, short and spraying down leg side, he sent it over the fine leg region. The one after that was pitched up and again met the treatment: slashed over the cover, one bounce and it went into the hands of the volunteers. To end the over, Samson converted a low full toss with the full face of his bat, knocked over the stumps at the non-striker's end and yet beat the fielder for a four!Even Rashid Khan was whacked for a four and a six before the Afghanistan spinner, and rest of the bowlers, perhaps, breathed a collective sigh of relief."It’s about just watching the ball and trying to get maximum out in the powerplay. Sometimes it works out well, sometimes it doesn’t. After a few failures, you definitely go through a lot. Being an Indian cricketer, it’s not easy to face failures, but that’s where my experience comes in," he said in the post-match press conference."I try to shut out the noise, try to be confident and come out and still keep scoring at a high strike rate, even taking the chances, even knowing that if I fail again, I will be facing a lot of noise. But I think that’s the way we are built here in Indian cricket. I just go out there and try to score maximum and contribute," he continued.As Samson took the crease in the first T20I, and not Sooryavanshi, the experts were divided. Kris Srikanth argued that Sooryavanshi "wasn't being treated properly". R Ashwin, meanwhile, implored the selectors, coaches and beyond to "understand his position." And yet, Samson gets how challenging making this call between the two is."It’s a very challenging place to be in. Right from the whole team management, the captain, coach and selectors. It’s a very tough choice, actually. All of them (himself, Sooryavanshi and Abhishek Sharma) are really good, all of them are performing, and all of them have to be given the right opportunity to keep performing at the international level," said Samson."It’s a very tough decision. I totally understand. I lead an IPL franchise, so I know how hard these decisions are, and everyone has been performing really well.""I have been in this kind of space for quite a few years, so I just know how to balance it out. Just think about what is in my control and try to be very positive with your competitors as well."I think they are competitors for the outside world, but we are a team and we are playing for a country. We want to win the game first, and then it comes down to the other individuals."We try to be as positive as possible, and whoever is playing, we want them to do well. We just have to be ready for our own opportunity. We can’t sulk or be in a negative frame of mind, thinking, 'Yaar, mujhe nahi mila, usko kyun diya?' Those kinds of mindsets don’t work here," he explained.For now, Samson has seemingly stalled the debate with a cracking knock in New Delhi. But whether it is enough to get a longer rope, with continued chances, remains to be seen.
Article Summary: Sanju Samson scored 57 runs from 22 balls, hitting seven fours and four sixes. He was benched unceremoniously after a poor showing against Ireland. He started the series with just 10 before producing the goods in the second contest. Azmatullah Omarzai and Mohammad Nabi bore the bulk of his prolific shot-making.

Article Text:
Grandmasters D Gukesh, R Praggnanandhaa and woman GM R Vaishali pose for photos at a felicitation ceremony after India won Gold medal in both open and women categories at the Chess Olympiad 2024. (PTI Photo)

How are pairings decided?

NEW DELHI: The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is being held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from September 15 to 27, with the opening ceremony already held and the first round on September 16.India enter the tournament as the defending champions in both the Open and Women’s sections, after creating history by winning both gold medals in Budapest in 2024. Around 200 national teams are competing across the two sections.The Olympiad is a team event played over 11 rounds under the Swiss system. Each team has five players, but only four play in any particular round, with the fifth available as a reserve. A match therefore consists of four individual games.A team win earns two match points, a draw one and a defeat none. The team with the most match points after 11 rounds wins the title.The competition is being played at the Silk Road International Exhibition Centre.Rounds 1 to 6 are scheduled from September 16 to 21, followed by a rest day on September 22.Rounds 7 to 11 will be played from September 23 to 27, with the closing ceremony on September 27. Games begin at 3pm local time, or 3.30pm IST, while the final round starts at 11am local time, or 11.30am IST.India's Open team is led by R Praggnanandhaa (2761) on Board 1, followed by Arjun Erigaisi (2759), Nihal Sarin (2718), world champion D Gukesh (2703) and Vidit Gujrathi (2697). Srinath Narayanan is the captain. India are seeded second in the Open section.The decision to place Gukesh on Board 4, after he played on top board in India's previous two Olympiads, is one of the major talking points. Praggnanandhaa will face the strongest opposition on Board 1, while the arrangement gives India considerable depth lower down the order.The women's team features Koneru Humpy, Divya Deshmukh, R Vaishali, Vantika Agrawal and Savitha Shri, with Swayams Mishra as captain. India are the top seeds in the women's section.India's biggest Open rivals include hosts Uzbekistan, USA and China, while Georgia, Kazakhstan, China and USA are among the leading challengers in the women's event. Uzbekistan, led by Javokhir Sindarov and Nodirbek Abdusattorov, will have home advantage.The Olympiad follows the Swiss system. The first-round pairings are based on team rankings, while subsequent opponents are determined by teams' results.Teams with similar scores are generally paired against each other, meaning India's opponents will become tougher if it keeps winning. No two teams can meet more than once. Each team fields four players in a match from its five-member squad.For India, the objective is straightforward but unprecedented: defend the double crown won in Budapest two years ago.
Article Summary: The 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad is being held in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, from September 15 to 27. India enter the tournament as the defending champions in both the Open and Women’s sections. Around 200 national teams are competing across the two sections.

Article Title: 'Don't make changes': Yuvraj Singh's warning to Gautam Gambhir and management ahead of 2027 World Cup
Article Text:
ROHIT SHARMA, VIRAT KOHLI

Yuvraj Singh warns against last-minute changes

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India's preparations for the 2027 ODI World Cup have already brought one major question into focus: what will their squad look like when the tournament gets underway in October?The World Cup will be staged in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, with India aiming to win the title for the third time after falling short in the 2023 final. With Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli having retired from the other formats of international cricket, their availability for the 50-over showpiece remains a key talking point.Amid the uncertainty, India's 2011 World Cup hero Yuvraj Singh has stressed the importance of one thing above all else: consistency.Speaking to Cricinfo, Yuvraj said India should settle on a core group of 16 to 20 players and give them regular opportunities in the limited number of ODIs available before the World Cup."They need to focus on building the same team to play in a year's time, because you don't want to make big changes at the last moment," Yuvraj Singh said.The former all-rounder believes regular game time will be particularly important with the ODI calendar becoming increasingly limited compared to T20 cricket."Whoever your players are, whether they are 16 or 20, it's important that everybody gets game time because obviously now there are more T20S and less 50-over cricket. Whatever matches there are, it's important that players get enough game time to prepare for the World Cup," he added.Yuvraj pointed to India's past struggles at major tournaments and argued that sudden changes close to a World Cup can disrupt a team's preparations."Every time India has faltered is when they've made some massive changes at the last moment or in the tournament. So I think it's important that we stick to a team that we believe can lift the 2027 World Cup and stick by those guys whether they fail or succeed till that moment.Belief in the squad is very important," Yuvraj further said.He also cited India's success in the 2024 and 2026 T20 World Cups as an example of how developing a settled group can help a team prepare for a major tournament. India also reached the 50-over World Cup final in 2023."That's something that we have also done in the last two T20 World Cups," Yuvraj said. "We also played the 50-over World Cup final [in 2023]. So we have had a lot of consistency in white-ball cricket. And that's what they need to do as well, to think of first qualifying for the semis and then going on to play in the last two [knockout matches]. I think that's a long way ahead. Focus should be on getting a squad ready, which is together and ready to fight in any situation," the star former all-rounder further went on to say.
Article Summary: India preparing for 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia. Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli have retired from other formats of international cricket. Yuvraj Singh says India should settle on a core group of 16 to 20 players.

Article Title: WPL 2027 auction likely on October 28 in Kochi
Article Text:
Royal Challengers Bengaluru's players celebrate with the trophy after winning the Women's Premier League (WPL) 2026 final T20 cricket match against Delhi Capitals, at Baroda Cricket Association Stadium, Kotambi in Vadodara, Gujarat. (PTI Photo/Kunal Patil)

Decision on Impact Player rule deferred to next month

MUMBAI: The Women's Premier League-2027 auction is likely to be conducted on October 29 in Kochi, TOI has learnt.The option of staging WPL 2027 matches in Varanasi, provided the stadium is ready by January next year, was discussed at Tuesday's WPL Governing Council meeting, which was held virtually."It has been decided that Mumbai's Brabourne Stadium will stage WPL-2027 matches. The second city for staging the WPL will be either Vadodara (Kotambi Stadium) or the new stadium in Varanasi. The BCCI is exploring the possibility of staging matches at Varanasi right now. A BCCI cricket operations team will conduct a recce of the Varanasi stadium, and assess whether it is ready or not to stage the tournament. Since it’s a new venue, we also need to conduct a few domestic/practice matches as well there," a source tracking developments told TOI on Wednesday.“The possibility of hosting WPL matches at the Chinnaswamy Stadium in Bengaluru was also discussed, but then it requires quite a few permissions from the local authorities,” the source informed.The historic Brabourne Stadium at the Cricket Club of India and the Kotambi Stadium in Vadodara will also stage the inaugural edition of the six-team ICC Women’s Champions Trophy 2027, with matches scheduled between Feb 14 and 28, 2027.In the past, the Brabourne Stadium has staged two WPL finals, in 2023 (inaugural season) and 2025, and missed out last year because new floodlights are being installed at the venue.The Brabourne Stadium is also the home venue of the Railways in the 2026-27 Ranji Trophy, and will stage three of their ties in the upcoming season.Vadodara staged the 2026 WPL final, in which the Smriti Mandhana-captained Royal Challengers Bengaluru beat Delhi Capitals by six wickets to lift the trophy.Meanwhile, at a meeting of the BCCI's IPL Governing Council on Tuesday, a decision on the controversial Impact Player rule in the IPL has been deferred to a meeting of the IPL GC next month."All the franchisees have submitted their feedback on the rule. That feedback will be assessed, and a final decision taken next month," a source added.It's learnt that a majority of the IPL franchises have voiced their reservations against the rule after the BCCI asked them to give their feedback about it.The debatable rule allows for an extra batter or bowler at any stage of the match, and has resulted in tall scores during the tournament, with batting line-ups becoming deeper.It has been argued that the rule is hurting the cause of the development of allrounders in Indian cricket.
Article Summary: The Women's Premier League-2027 auction is likely to be conducted on October 29 in Kochi. The option of staging WPL 2027 matches in Varanasi, provided the stadium is ready by January next year, was discussed at Tuesday's WPL Governing Council meeting. Decision on Impact Player rule deferred to next month.

Article Title: Chess Olympiad: Uzbeks face tough test from defending champs India
Article Text:
Chess Olympiad in Samarkand (FIDE Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Former champions Uzbekistan will be severely tested as their men will try to regain the Olympiad chess title that they won in India four years ago.Uzbekistan will feel the added pressure of home expectations at Samarkand coupled with the might of defending champions India in the 11-round over-the-board classical tournament. They had stopped India's winning spree with draws in 2022 and 2024 editions of the biennial team event. Their then captain Vladimir Kramnik had dubbed the match two years ago in Budapest as "real chess" (all-drawn games with no blunders) when other teams crumbled against marauding individual gold medallists D Gukesh on the top board and Erigaisi Arjun on the third.Most importantly, the 46th Olympiad - with record 399 teams across two sections - also provides Gukesh a chance to regain his form in the team atmosphere with the motivation of playing for the tricolour before his title defence against Sindarov in Geneva that starts on Nov 24. In the last two Olympiads, he was the player of the tournament before winning the world crown at age 18 in late 2024 that seems to be weighing heavy on his shoulders.Now captained by V Anand's former second Rustam Kasimdzhanov, Uzbeks have the new chess star Javokhir Sindarov as their top rated player, a world No. 4 at 2778. "It was unimaginable that we would host an event of this magnitude six-seven years ago," said Nodirbek Abdusarttorov (age 21) at a press conference on Tuesday."But thanks to the support and hard work of players, it is made possible."India had won the double gold in both sections last time. They too have high expectations to deal with. The women's team, comprising K Humpy, World Cup winner Divya Deshmukh and world championship challenger R Vaishali are the top seeds because Russia remains banned from team competitions and China have not sent their full-strength team. And despite having the most exciting trinity - of world champion D Gukesh, in-form R Praggnanandhaa and Arjun - in their ranks, the Indian men are not the top seeds in the open event. That honour belongs to the USA, comprising Fabiano Caruna (formerly Italy), Wesley So (formerly Philippines) and Levon Aronian (formerly Armenia) among others.
Article Summary: Former champions Uzbekistan will be severely tested as their men will try to regain the Olympiad chess title that they won in India four years ago. They had stopped India's winning spree with draws in 2022 and 2024 editions of the biennial team event. India had won the double gold in both sections last time.

NEW DELHI: With the majority of first-choice ODI players busy at the Asian Games and a host of players nursing injuries, it’s going to be a heady day for the national selectors here on Wednesday as they meet to pick the ODI team for the three-match home series against West Indies from Sept 27.TOI understands selectors are expected to spend a lot of time discussing whether they want to bring back Ravindra Jadeja , as Axar Patel will be on Asian Games duty. The other big call will be to decide on the second wicketkeeper, with KL Rahul and Hardik Pandya’s availability also a factor.It is learnt that the team management and the selectors want to move on from Jadeja. However, with Axar’s unavailability and Harsh Dubey injured, the selectors may consider Jadeja for ODIs.“Jadeja’s bowling in white-ball cricket hasn’t been up to the mark for a while now. Dubey was identified as Axar’s backup. The other spin-bowling allrounder, Washington Sundar, too will be at the Asian Games. The team management wants an established batter in the middle order,” a BCCI source told TOI.In the case of Pandya, the Centre of Excellence (CoE) has shared a report which says the star allrounder should be fit for competitive cricket from Sept 20.The selectors had named him in the 50-over India ‘A’ team for the series against Australia ‘A’, which starts on Oct 6.TOI has learnt that Pandya himself doesn’t want to rush back to international cricket until he is absolutely convinced about his fitness, which will allow him to bowl 10 overs in a match. The other two seam-bowling allrounders, Nitish Kumar Reddy and Shivam Dube, too will be in Japan. It is learnt that Suryansh Shedge is also nursing an injury.TOI has learnt that the selectors are keen to give Rishabh Pant another go in the ODI format since Ishan Kishan will be at the Asian Games. Pant will be facing competition from Dhruv Jurel.“The selectors feel that Pant has the game against pace and bounce which can be useful in South Africa. He is more experienced than Jurel,” the source said.
Article Summary: India selectors meet to pick the ODI team for the three-match home series against West Indies from Sept 27. The majority of first-choice ODI players are busy at the Asian Games. The other big call will be to decide on the second wicketkeeper with KL Rahul and Hardik Pandya’s availability also a factor.

Article Title: Carrying India’s basketball dream to Asian Games, referee Rakesh to make his Asiad debut even as no Indian team will take court
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

CHENNAI: While India has no basketball team at the Asian Games, R Rakesh is the country’s sole representative in the sport as a referee. The Aichi-Nagoya Games will mark his debut in Asian Games, the Karnataka man earlier appearing for Asian championships.The 36-year-old became a FIBA referee at the age of 23 and has a vast experience for over a decade. “Till now (in the current edition), I have officiated on almost all the days. At the Asian Championships last year in China, I officiated until the semifinals. Since it was my maiden edition, I could not proceed further. There have been many ups and downs in my journey. In some tournaments, I get to officiate in the final, but in some, I do not even get to officiate in the semifinals. It depends on the performance, and that is common in sports,” Rakesh told TOI from Japan.Rakesh, currently India’s only elite-level referee, said lack of monetary benefit is one of the reasons behind the lack of quality Indian officials. “How long can a referee manage to officiate in matches without much monetary benefit? Passion can only push a person to a certain point. Why do people prefer cricket? It is because of the monetary benefits.We need to have leagues, more international matches in India and popularise the sport. ...Initially, I also struggled and used to do only domestic matches. Sometimes, tournaments used to get cancelled in rainy seasons and at times due to lack of sponsorships the tournaments got scrapped. However, now I get to officiate regularly,” Rakesh added.Rakesh has officiated in multiple leagues across Asia, including in the Philippines, Lebanon, Syria and Indonesia. He has also been officiating in the Maldives league for the past 10 years. In 2018, he received an opportunity to officiate at the World Junior NBA Championships in Miami.
Article Summary: India has no basketball team at the Asian Games. R Rakesh is the country’s sole representative in the sport as a referee. The 36-year-old became a FIBA referee at the age of 23 and has a vast experience for over a decade.

Article Title: Seven months pregnant, she judged bouts. Now, history awaits Kirtisna at 2026 Asian Games
Article Text:
Kirtisna Arya

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: There is one image from her wrestling journey that Kirtisna Arya remembers with unusual clarity. It was May 2023. She was in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, for the South East Asian (SEA) Games, seven months pregnant with her second child.While most expectant mothers would have been preparing for the final stretch of pregnancy, Kirtisna was spending five consecutive days on a wrestling mat, demonstrating her officiating and judging skills as part of her United World Wrestling (UWW) coaching examination.The examination could not wait. Neither could she. “I was seven months pregnant (with son Darsh) was when I appeared for the Category 1 Level 1 course. For four-five days continuously, I had to be on the mat and demonstrate my skills. I was pregnant, but I was determined to complete the course,” Kirtisna recalls.That determination, more than three years later, has taken the 37-year-old from Uttarakhand to Nagoya — Kirtisna will become the first Indian woman to officiate at the Games, or any of the other major multisport events.Accredited as technical official, Kirtisna will shoulder three responsibilities during the Games: referee bouts, judge matches and serve as mat chairman.“When I received the mail from UWW informing me about my selection, it was a proud moment for the family. My daughter Pannavi was overjoyed,” Kirtisna told TOI.“I never thought I would be selected for the Asian Games,” she said.Krirtisna will leave for Japan on Sept 26. The assignment will keep her away from home for around 10 days, including from three-and-a-half-year-old Darsh. “I know it will be difficult for them, but they will understand what their mother did when they grow up and hopefully take pride in it,” she said.For Kirtisna, the road to Japan has never been about reaching one particular destination. It has been about refusing to step away from wrestling — even when life repeatedly gave her reasons to do so.Kirtisna grew up in Bharatpur village in Haridwar district, in a family where wrestling was deeply woven into everyday life. Father Omveer Singh was a renowned wrestler and a disciple of the legendary Master Chandgi Ram. Yet having a wrestler for a father did not necessarily make it easy for the daughters to become wrestlers. “People would say, ‘Girls are not meant for wrestling. Don’t put your girls there.’ There was a lot of societal pressure,” Kirtisna says.Yet, Kirtisna, the second of three sisters, began wrestling in 2004 after Class X, and her biggest achievement on the mat came at the 2011 Commonwealth Championships in Melbourne, where she won silver in the 59kg category.An ACL tear brought end to her playing career and she quit wrestling in 2013. She completed an NIS coaching diploma in 2010-11 and, in Feb 2014, joined the SAI centre in Bahalgarh, Sonepat, as an assistant coach. Motherhood brought a fresh challenge. Her daughter Pannavi was born in 2016 and that led her to switch to refereeing.
Article Summary: Kirtisna Arya will become the first Indian woman to officiate at the Asian Games. The 37-year-old will referee bouts, judge matches and serve as mat chairman. Arya won silver at the 2011 Commonwealth Championships in Melbourne.

BENGALURU: World No. 1 men’s javelin thrower Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage’s gold hunt at the Asian Games hit an air pocket on Tuesday. His famous javelins, which flew to 92.62m on June 4 at the Diamond League in Rome, 92.07m on Aug 27 at the Diamond League in Zurich, and 91.09m on Sunday at the WA Ultimate Championship in Budapest, were all found damaged when he returned to Colombo as the new king of javelin.“All three javelins I used for over 90 throws have been damaged. It might have been a mistake by the airline, but that’s how it is. It’s not a big issue. I’ll move on,” the Sri Lankan star told reporters at Colombo airport after travelling on a Turkish Airlines flight. The 23-year-old has had an outstanding season this year, becoming the first Ultimate Champion, winning the Diamond League finals and climbing to the top of the world rankings.After starting his season with an 89.37m effort in the suburbs of Colombo, the Sri Lankan served notice by winning the Rome Diamond League with a monstrous 92.62m effort. This went perilously close to the 92.97m Arshad Nadeem of Pakistan threw to win Paris Olympics gold while setting a new Olympic and Asian record.Recognising the potential of their latest star, the Sri Lankan sports minister said the Lankan govt will provide Tharanga with a new set of javelins, the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports was quoted by News Wire, a news outlet from the island nation.“Our govt will continue to stand behind our athletics star and his Olympic dream,” the minister said. “The govt is also considering seeking compensation from the airline over the damage, while looking into possible legal and diplomatic measures,” according to the ministry.Pathirage, who won the bronze with a best of 84.34m at Neeraj Chopra Classic at Sree Kanteerava Stadium here in July last year, has improved by leaps and bounds this year. He won the Diamond League finals, beating the likes of 2012 London Olympics and 2025 World champion Keshorn Walcott of Trinidad and Tobago.He won five Diamond League meets, and one of his rare defeats came in May, when he finished second to Anderson Peters of Grenada in Rabat. Commonwealth Games in Glasgow were expected to be the big battle between Pathirage, Olympic champion Nadeem and India's superstar Neeraj Chopra and Yash Vir Singh to grab the gold. The battle between Chopra, Nadeem and Pathirage was expected to resume at the Asiad in Paloha Mizuho Stadium in Nagoya. But with Chopra forced to end his season due to injury and Arshad not in great form either, the Sri Lankan will start as the overwhelming favourite.

Article Title: It's Japan time: A gold double in cricket appears a given, but it will provide benchmark for LA Olympics

When the United States men’s basketball team goes to the Olympics, they face a unique situation. For the NBA superstars, a gold is a given, anything less is a fall from grace.The Indian cricket contingent at the Asian Games will feel a bit like the ‘Dream Teams’. Two gold medals appear a foregone conclusion and there would probably be any euphoria when it happens. But just in case it’s a silver for either of the star-studded teams which are products of the cash-rich IPL and WPL, the backlash will be quite significant.On the face of it, there’s no reason for any worry for those who will be tracking the Indian teams. The men have got a bye in the first round and their first match is a quarterfinal — in all probability against Nepal. If all goes to plan, Sri Lanka and Pakistan will be their next two rivals at the Korogi Sports Park — the ground built from scratch.Matches will be day games with Indian men’s matches starting at 1.30 pm local time. While Nepal is a bit of an unknown quantity, the other teams get beaten by India as a matter of habit across tournaments, be it the T20 World Cup, Asia Cup or the rare bilateral tournament.Despite the tag of overwhelming favourites, the sports ministry and the BCCI aren’t taking any chances.There was the option of sending a second-string team, but even Jasprit Bumrah, coming back from an injury lay-off, is headed to Japan. There were issues about five-star accommodation for the superstars, but that too has been taken care of to keep all the parties happy.While there’s the obligation of winning gold, there’s another angle to this Indian campaign. Cricket will be back in the Olympics at Los Angeles two years down the line after a gap of 128 years, and the success of the return hinges on how India perform.It is the Indian diaspora around the world that fuels the sport and such has been the domination of the Men in Blue in T20 cricket of late, that anything other than the champions’ medal is a huge dampener for this group of globe-trotting cheerleaders.Many of them will be at Aichi-Nagoya as well and in addition to the gold, there will be another demand from them — to witness some Vaibhav Sooryavanshi blitzkrieg.With the next T20 World Cup and the Olympics still a couple of years away, this Asian Games can also be a bit of a test for two T20 specialists Shivam Dube and Varun Chakravarthy, provided the spinner passes the fitness test following the side strain that he suffered during the Afghanistan series. They have been a slight up and down of late and there’s a chance that if they don’t get their acts right, this could be their last Indian stints for the time being.But before the men start their campaign, it’s the girls who will get the ball rolling. The women’s tournament will be a good indication as to how the conditions will be in this new venue. Harmanpreet Kaur’s girls are going to Japan on the back of a crushing Asia Cup victory, where they have walked past all the teams.There’s no reason to believe anything different will happen at Aichi-Nagoya as the men and women will look to lend a golden hue to the Indian campaign in addition to adding new fans for the sport itself with their dynamism.

NEW DELHI: Sanju Samson has spent years learning to live with the scrutiny that comes with playing for India. On Tuesday, after his 57 off 22 balls against Afghanistan in the second T20I, he admitted that the noise from outside does get through — even if his preferred response is to switch it off.“I try to switch the Wi-Fi off. But sometimes the Wi-Fi gets switched on and comments become visible,” Samson said after India’s seven-wicket win. “Some senior player says something. So I think it’s very normal.”Samson’s innings, in which 52 of his 57 runs came in boundaries, came at a time when his place at the top of India’s T20I order is under scrutiny. The emergence of 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has added another layer to the competition for the two opening slots alongside Abhishek Sharma . Sooryavanshi had impressed on India’s recent tour of Zimbabwe, while Samson had been left out of that series after failing to convert his opportunities in the preceding Ireland, England series."Definitely, outside noise does affect cricketers in India,” Samson said. “But you need to be very clear about what your mindset is, how you need to prepare and what mindset you need to play with."“I think I have been mature enough and experienced enough to know how to handle it. Earlier, it used to hurt a little. I’m not a machine. We are not robots that we can say, ‘No, it doesn’t affect me.’ Definitely, it affects you,” he said.“If I paid attention to those things, I couldn’t bat like this,” Samson said. “Before hitting a shot, I would think ten times, ‘Yaar, out ho gaya toh phir Wi-Fi problem ho jayega.’ So instead, I tell myself, ‘Koi baat nahi.’”That mindset has become particularly important as Samson finds himself competing for a place with a teenager who has rapidly forced his way into the conversation. Samson, however, said he does not view Sooryavanshi as a rival within the dressing room.“I think they (Sooryavanshi and Abhishek Sharma) are competitors for the outside world, but we are a team and we are playing for a country,” he said. “We want to win the game first, and then it comes down to the other individuals.”Samson also said his experience as an IPL captain has helped him understand why difficult selection calls have to be made. He acknowledged that the management has a difficult task in choosing between players who are all performing, while stressing that individuals have to remain ready for their opportunities rather than dwell on selection decisions.“We can’t sulk or be in a negative frame of mind, thinking, ‘Yaar, mujhe nahi mila, usko kyun diya.’ Those kinds of mindsets don’t work here,” he said.
Article Summary: Sanju Samson has spent years learning to live with the scrutiny that comes with playing for India. He admitted that the noise from outside does get through — even if his preferred response is to switch it off. Samson’s innings, in which 52 of his 57 runs came in boundaries, came at a time when his place at the top of the T20I order is under scrutiny.

NEW DELHI: It's not easy being Sanju Samson . He has been forever walking the line in his 10-year-old international career, partly because of team dynamics and mostly because of his unignorable inconsistency. As he has often done in his career when pushed to a corner, he served a reminder on Tuesday night in the second T20I against Afghanistan why it's difficult to dismiss his potential in T20 cricket In a matter of seven overs, after the Indian bowlers expectedly restricted Afghanistan to a modest 159/8 on evidently sluggish pitch, Samson buried the ghosts of the Ireland and England tour with 57 off 22 balls in a cold and merciless spell of ball-striking. In doing so, he virtually killed the game, setting the stage for Ishan to ease to an unbeaten 38 off 23 balls for India to canter to a series victory with a seven-wicket win in 14.5 overs.In the first two T20Is, India's two preferred T20I openers Abhishek Sharma and Samson regained their form after a lull post the victorious T20 World Cup campaign at home in March. Nitish Kumar Reddy bowling three overs for 3/24 would settle a few nerves in the team management which is fretting over zeroing on a seam-bowling allrounder in the white-ball format.With no major T20I assignment, barring the Asian Games later this month, lined up before 2028, this series bore very little significance.Yet, it was a series that could have determined Samson's international future. This was a banana peel series for him. He couldn't afford to have slipped here, certainly not when there is an eagerness to give 16-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi a long run. He was done in by his inconsistency in the UK two months ago where he failed to get started in four T20Is he played, forcing the team management to hand Sooryavanshi an international debut.Samson's poker face and unassuming demanour at the crease, doesn't give away his destructive ability with the willow in hand. With each of his four sixes and seven boundaries, he went about demolishing Afghanistan's spin-bowling strength in the Powerplay and dismissing doubts over his capability as a T20 batter in Indian conditions.As Samson played the dominant hand in the 88-run opening partnership in 6.2 overs before Abhishek holed out at deep mid-wicket off Sanju Samson for 39 off 19, the duo reminded the world of the treachery they could inflict on bowling attacks up front in the innings.The pitch here doesn't resemble the hard and flat concrete-like decks India played in India during the T20 World Cup. This one is tired after hosting incessant cricket for nearly a year. Afghanistan's spin attack of Mohammed Nabi, Rashid Khan, Mujeeb Ur Rahman and Noor Ahmad have fetched premium value in T20 leagues around the globe with their unconventional style of bowling. Afghanistan, trailing in the three-match series, didn't leave anything to chance and unleashed their most lethal weapons together up front in the second innings.The pitch did show signs of holding up and taking considerable turn in the latter half of the chase, but Samson decided to eliminate the threat before holing out to Rashid centimeters from the long-off boundary.Now that the series is sealed, it will be interesting see if India give Sooryavanshi another hit in the third T20I on Thursday. For now, though, Samson and Abhishek have ensured the teenager will have to push harder to establish himself in this batting lineup.
Article Summary: Sanju Samson scored 57 off 22 balls in second T20I against Afghanistan. India won the three-match series 1-0 with a seven-wicket win in 14.5 overs. The 10-year-old has been forever walking the line in his international career. He served a reminder on Tuesday night of his potential in T20 cricket.

NEW DELHI: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey, with the state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house.The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal.Dey won the women’s -48kg title in Glasgow after defeating Canada’s Heidi Quach in a dramatic golden-score contest. The state government also presented her with a cheque of Rs 10 lakh as part of the felicitation.Speaking at the event, Saha highlighted Dey’s difficult journey from a small village in South Tripura to the top of the Commonwealth Games podium. Her father, he noted, worked as a cycle mechanic in Sonaichari.“The journey from an obscure village in South Tripura to a podium finish at Glasgow was a race against time. Her father was a cycle mechanic at Sonaichari. Against all odds, she stood firm on her mission and achieved phenomenal success for the country,” he said.The chief minister recalled meeting Dey at Tripura Bhavan in New Delhi after her return from the Games.During that meeting, the judoka had expressed her wish to have a house in Agartala.“During the meeting, Asmita revealed she desperately wanted a house in Agartala. I promised to fulfil her wish, and today a piece of land has been allotted to her,” he said.Saha said Dey’s achievement could motivate more young athletes from Tripura to pursue sport at the highest level. He also urged her to remain disciplined as she prepares for the Asian Games, particularly because of the strict anti-doping requirements.“I urge Asmita to remain alert, particularly about food, because she has to pass through a stringent dope test before joining the prestigious Asian Games. We believe she will shine again in the Asian Games by winning a medal for the country,” he said.Youth Affairs and Sports Minister Tinku Roy, Agartala Mayor Dipak Majumder and Arjuna award-winning gymnast Dipa Karmakar were among those who attended the felicitation ceremony.
Article Summary: Tripura chief minister Manik Saha has fulfilled a promise made to Commonwealth Games gold medallist Asmita Dey. The state government allotting her a piece of land in Agartala to build a house. The 23-year-old judoka was honoured in Tripura on Wednesday after becoming the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth games gold medal.

Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

Article Title: ‘That video was not ordinary’: PM Modi praises Lovlina for objecting to distorted India map - Watch
Article Text:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi shares a light moment with boxer Lovlina Borgohain. (PTI Photo)

‘That video was not ordinary’

Mirabai opens up about four difficult years

Narender's joke leaves Modi laughing

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

Article Title: ‘From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping’: PM Modi’s heartfelt message to CWG heroes - Watch
Article Text:
PM Narendra Modi interacted with India's CWG 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday. (Pic credit: PM Modi's X post)

Mirabai recalls four years of struggle

‘One family will bring three medals’

India’s Glasgow success

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.
Article Summary: PM Narendra Modi hosted medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg. Modi heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze.

Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:
India's Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

The Sports Ministry hurdle

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:
India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit (PTI Photo)

Invited, but left waiting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place.
